title: Fertility-preserving interception of high-grade serous tubo-ovarian carcinoma

concept.text: Proposed innovation: prevent invasive high-grade serous tubo-ovarian carcinoma by finding and stopping a precursor in the fallopian tube while preserving the tube’s reproductive function. The intervention would need to reach people outside the population already undergoing pelvic surgery and ultimately demonstrate fewer deaths from this cancer. Its mechanism remains unspecified: identifying a precursor would be useful only if it enabled a safe, effective intervention.

The proposed advance combines three requirements that the supplied studies do not demonstrate together: prevention before invasive cancer, retained tubal fertility, and reduced mortality. Opportunistic bilateral salpingectomy removes the fallopian tubes during another pelvic operation while conserving the ovaries; its observational prevention evidence therefore concerns a different intervention. UKCTOCS tested screening in postmenopausal women, rather than fertility-preserving treatment of a tubal precursor.

significance.text: The potential importance rests on a substantial cancer burden and the difficulty of translating earlier diagnosis into longer life. The supplied salpingectomy article describes high-grade serous carcinoma as accounting for approximately 70% of ovarian carcinomas and describes five-year survival for ovarian carcinoma overall as below 50%. UKCTOCS describes most ovarian cancers as presenting with advanced disease. These statements support the preventive rationale, but they do not establish that high-grade serous carcinoma is the most lethal subtype or separately quantify its frequency of late presentation.

Conditional significance: an intervention that demonstrably prevents high-grade serous cancer deaths while retaining tubal fertility would create a major preventive capability. Delivery beyond incidental pelvic surgery could extend that benefit to people who would otherwise never encounter an opportunity for surgical prevention. The direct benefit would be fewer deaths in the population shown to benefit; the size of any broader population effect would also depend on eligibility, uptake, delivery capacity, durability, and harms.

UKCTOCS makes the distinction between stage at diagnosis and mortality especially important. Its multimodal screening approach increased early-stage detection without demonstrating a significant reduction in ovarian and tubal cancer deaths. This result supports requiring a mortality outcome for the proposed innovation. It does not establish that every future screening or precursor-interception strategy must fail.

Conceptual analogy: the ambition resembles cervical-cancer prevention through vaccination and precursor treatment, in the broad sense of acting before invasive disease. The supplied sources do not document that history or establish an equivalent biological target, accessible sampling route, or preventive tool for tubo-ovarian carcinoma. The analogy conveys the desired transformation rather than evidence of feasibility. Treatment of metastatic disease remains a separate advance, and this concept does not depend on a blood test exceeding 95% sensitivity and specificity.

missing_breakthrough.text: Proposed missing capability: a practical intervention must identify or otherwise act on a tubal precursor early enough to prevent invasive high-grade serous carcinoma, preserve functional tubal fertility, and produce a measurable mortality benefit. The supplied evidence motivates this goal but does not establish a feasible interception mechanism or verify whether such a capability remains unavailable as of November 1, 2026.

The research characterizes the target precursor as microscopic and located inside an organ that is not routinely sampled. Those anatomical and sampling assertions were not established by the retained source passages and should remain provisional here. The concrete research questions are whether the relevant precursor can be reached or recognized reliably, whether it can be distinguished from changes that would never progress, and whether intervention can occur before invasive spread. The supplied evidence does not resolve the full precursor model or its tractability.

Proposed engineering barriers include delivering treatment to the relevant tissue, eliminating or controlling the dangerous lesion, and preserving the function needed for tubal conception. Ovarian conservation alone would not establish this outcome: the salpingectomy study defines an operation that preserves ovaries while removing the tubes. A tube-preserving approach would need its own evidence of local effectiveness, reproductive safety, and durable protection.

The evidentiary barrier is also substantial. UKCTOCS shows that a favorable stage shift can occur without a demonstrated mortality benefit, while the salpingectomy study supplies an observational association with cancer incidence. Neither result establishes that treating a precursor while retaining the tubes will prevent deaths. A successful program would need to connect target engagement, prevention of invasive high-grade serous disease, retained fertility, and long-term clinical benefit.

current_state.text: The 2021 UK Collaborative Trial of Ovarian Cancer Screening report in The Lancet described a median follow-up of 16.3 years. Multimodal screening increased early-stage detection, but no statistically significant reduction in ovarian and tubal cancer deaths was observed; the authors did not recommend general population screening using those approaches. The trial concerned postmenopausal women and ovarian and tubal cancer mortality, rather than a high-grade-serous-specific, fertility-preserving precursor intervention. The supplied review relied on the retained PubMed abstract, not the full paper.

On February 2, 2026, Sowamber, Hanley, Huntsman, and colleagues reported a population-based retrospective cohort analysis in JAMA Network Open, volume 9, article e2557267. Opportunistic bilateral salpingectomy was associated with a crude hazard ratio of 0.22 for serous ovarian carcinoma compared with comparison surgery, with a 95% confidence interval of 0.05–0.95. The analysis combined low- and high-grade serous cancers and measured incidence, not mortality. The wide interval indicates substantial uncertainty, and the authors acknowledged that they could not control all possible confounders. This association supports a preventive rationale for tube removal without proving the proposed fertility-preserving interception.

The earlier research reported five cancer cases in the salpingectomy group, but that count could not be verified from the retained extraction. The supplied review had article prose but lacked the table contents, figure graphics, and supplementary material needed to resolve that detail. The count therefore remains unconfirmed; this extraction limitation does not negate the supported hazard ratio and confidence interval or demonstrate that the count is false.

The research also cited a 2026 JAMA European consensus as supporting the offer of opportunistic salpingectomy during other surgery and described its access as abstract-level. No document or retained text for that citation was available to the supplied review, so its identity, wording, and recommendation could not be verified. Independently, the reviewed salpingectomy study defines the opportunistic approach as tube removal during another pelvic operation. That definition does not imply that standalone salpingectomy is impossible, and neither approach demonstrates preservation of the tubes.

The supplied record establishes these dated screening and surgical findings, but contains no demonstration of the full proposed innovation. Its freshness-search record is empty, so it cannot establish the complete state of the field on November 1, 2026. The absence of a demonstration in these materials should not be treated as proof that no other intervention or relevant result exists.

completion_criteria.text: Proposed decisive demonstration: a prospective controlled evaluation, preferably randomized where feasible, should show fewer deaths from high-grade serous tubo-ovarian carcinoma in a population recruited beyond people already undergoing unrelated pelvic surgery. Mortality should be specified as a primary outcome with sufficient follow-up and statistical precision to assess benefit. Earlier diagnosis, a stage shift, or lower incidence alone would provide useful intermediate evidence but would not satisfy this proposed mortality criterion. This choice is motivated by UKCTOCS rather than presented as an established consensus standard.
completion_criteria.label: Reduced high-grade serous tubo-ovarian carcinoma mortality beyond pelvic-surgery populations

completion_criteria.text: Proposed fertility demonstration: participants who wish to retain tubal fertility should retain functional reproductive capacity after intervention. Assessment should distinguish anatomical tube preservation, ovarian function, and actual fertility outcomes, including pregnancy outcomes where participants attempt conception. Reliance on assisted reproduction would not by itself establish retained tubal fertility. The protocol should account for baseline fertility, reproductive intentions, and other causes of infertility rather than interpreting every failure to conceive as an intervention effect.
completion_criteria.label: Retained functional tubal fertility demonstrated through actual reproductive outcomes

completion_criteria.text: Proposed supporting evidence should show that the intervention reaches its intended precursor, prevents progression without unacceptable tissue injury, and provides durable protection. Safety assessment should include unnecessary interventions, reproductive harms, and burdens created by repeated testing or treatment. No fixed sensitivity, specificity, or other numerical threshold is adopted here; acceptable performance would need justification in the intended population and delivery setting.
completion_criteria.label: Durable prevention of intended precursor progression without unacceptable tissue injury

completion_criteria.text: Proposed reproducibility and practical boundaries: independent teams and multiple clinical settings should reproduce benefit with a clearly specified intervention, eligibility rules, and follow-up procedures. Reports should define the ages, risk groups, histotypes, and reproductive circumstances actually studied, together with access requirements and residual cancer risk. Success in finite studies would establish demonstrated breadth within those conditions, not universal protection or effectiveness for every ovarian cancer subtype.
completion_criteria.label: Independently reproduced benefit across clinical settings with reported practical boundaries

related_concepts.text: Roster-based synthesis: OBG-02, Manufacture of a functional human oocyte from a somatic cell, and OBG-05, Reversal of human ovarian reproductive aging, overlap through the goal of retaining or expanding reproductive opportunity. Their targets are oocyte production and ovarian aging, respectively; OBG-09 targets cancer prevention while preserving tubal function. Success in one would not establish success in the others.

Roster-based synthesis: OBG-07, A mechanism-based cure for endometriosis, shares the ambition of treating gynecologic disease while potentially protecting fertility. Its disease target and required causal mechanism differ from interception of a cancer precursor. OBG-08, A manufactured uterus that supports pregnancy without a donor graft and chronic immunosuppression, concerns uterine gestational capacity; retaining fallopian-tube function does not create or replace that capacity.

Roster-based synthesis: OBG-01, Causal control of the human parturition clock; OBG-04, In utero reversal of placental insufficiency; and OBG-10, Restoration of the amniotic compartment after preterm membrane rupture, concern mechanisms and complications of an established pregnancy. They share an organ-preserving therapeutic ambition with OBG-09, but their targets and outcomes differ from prevention of invasive carcinoma and cancer death.

Roster-based synthesis: OBG-03, Extrauterine physiological support across the viability gap, concerns support of development outside the uterus, while OBG-06, In utero molecular correction of fetal-onset genetic disease, concerns treatment of fetal disease. Both overlap with OBG-09 at the broad level of reproductive medicine. Neither addresses tubal precursor interception, and OBG-09 does not imply extrauterine support or fetal genetic correction.

change_log.change: Preserved OBG-09 and its title while defining the innovation as a proposed combination of precursor interception, retained tubal fertility, delivery beyond incidental surgery, and mortality reduction.
change_log.reason: The evidence motivates the concept without demonstrating that the combined capability has been achieved.

change_log.change: Replaced the unsupported lethality ranking with the supported estimate that high-grade serous carcinoma accounts for approximately 70% of ovarian carcinomas; confined advanced-presentation and survival statements to ovarian cancer overall.
change_log.reason: The retained evidence does not support the original subtype-specific lethality and presentation claims.

change_log.change: Preserved UKCTOCS's 16.3-year median follow-up and mortality finding while specifying its postmenopausal population, outcome scope, and abstract-only review access.
change_log.reason: Its screening result should not be generalized to every future early-detection strategy or treated as a direct fertility-preserving interception trial.

change_log.change: Retained the 2026 salpingectomy hazard ratio and confidence interval, and clarified that the retrospective analysis combined low- and high-grade serous cancers and measured incidence.
change_log.reason: The association does not establish a high-grade-serous-specific mortality benefit or eliminate confounding.

change_log.change: Preserved the reported five-case count as unconfirmed and explained the missing table and supplementary evidence.
change_log.reason: The supplied extraction cannot verify the count, but its absence is not evidence that the count is false.

change_log.change: Qualified the cited European consensus and corrected the implication that tube removal can occur only during another operation.
change_log.reason: No consensus artifact was retained, and the restriction to another operation defines the opportunistic approach rather than all salpingectomy.

change_log.change: Recast microscopic precursor, sampling, and present-day availability assertions as unresolved questions rather than established facts.
change_log.reason: The retained passages do not establish those assertions, and the freshness-search record is empty.

change_log.change: Retained the cervical-cancer analogy as a limited conceptual comparison and expanded proposed demonstrations of fertility, safety, reproducibility, and practical scope.
change_log.reason: The analogy does not establish biological equivalence, and the completion criteria must remain explicitly proposed rather than attributed to published standards.

change_log.change: Added distinctions connecting OBG-09 with every other supplied roster entry.
change_log.reason: Related reproductive goals do not justify merging concepts with different biological targets and completion requirements.

unresolved_issues: Whether a population-deliverable, fertility-preserving precursor intervention was available or had relevant clinical results by November 1, 2026 remains unassessed because the supplied freshness-search record is empty.
The precursor's microscopic characteristics, accessibility, routine sampling context, progression risk, and actionable treatment window are not established by the supplied retained passages.
The claimed five cases in the salpingectomy group require verification against the original table or other complete source material.
The identity, exact recommendation, and scope of the cited 2026 European consensus require a retained source; the earlier description of abstract-level access cannot resolve them.
The intervention mechanism, delivery route, durability, eligible population, and capacity to preserve functional tubal fertility remain unspecified.

The relationship between the observed reduction in combined serous cancer incidence after salpingectomy and a mortality benefit from tube-preserving high-grade serous precursor interception remains to be demonstrated.
Trial duration, sample size, acceptable harms, fertility measures, and clinically meaningful benefit thresholds require prospective justification; none is established by the supplied evidence.

brief.title: Preventing ovarian cancer while preserving fertility
possible: People could prevent a common form of ovarian cancer while keeping the ability to conceive through their fallopian tubes, the organs whose reproductive function treatment would preserve. The goal is to stop an early change before it becomes invasive cancer.

This prevention could reach people who are not already having pelvic surgery. Success would mean fewer deaths from high-grade serous carcinoma, the cancer targeted here, alongside preserved fertility.
why: Most ovarian cancers are diagnosed after the disease has advanced. Preventing cancer before it invades could spare people a life-threatening illness while preserving their reproductive choices.

sources.showed: A randomized trial in women after menopause found that screening increased early-stage detection without significantly reducing deaths from ovarian and fallopian tube cancers.
sources.cited_for: Earlier diagnosis alone does not establish that a prevention strategy saves lives.
sources.not_established: The trial did not test treatment of an early change in the fallopian tube while preserving fertility.

sources.who: Ramlogan Sowamber, Gillian Hanley, David Huntsman and colleagues
sources.showed: An observational study linked tube removal to fewer serous ovarian cancers. A separate comparison found a smaller share of high-grade serous carcinoma (HGSC) among ovarian cancers in people without tubes.
sources.quote: Our second aim showed significantly fewer HGSCs in people without fallopian tubes compared with the historical histotype distribution for ovarian carcinoma.
sources.cited_for: Removing fallopian tubes supports the case for preventing cancer by acting there.
sources.not_established: The study did not establish fewer deaths or preserved tubal fertility, and other differences between groups could affect the association.

sources.showed: This is a European consensus concerning the offer of fallopian tube removal during other pelvic surgery.
sources.cited_for: It concerns surgical prevention through fallopian tube removal.
sources.not_established: Tube removal does not demonstrate prevention that preserves the tubes and their reproductive function.

shown: Sowamber and colleagues found an association between tube removal and fewer serous ovarian cancers. Cancer cases were few, and the study could not account for all differences between groups. It measured cancer occurrence, not deaths.

Menon and colleagues showed that screening can find more cancers early without demonstrating fewer deaths. Together, these studies support pursuing prevention and measuring whether it actually saves lives.
missing: A treatment must stop a precursor, an early change that can become cancer, while keeping the fallopian tubes functional.
Actual pregnancy outcomes must establish that treatment preserves the ability to conceive through the tubes.
Controlled studies must demonstrate fewer deaths, including among people recruited beyond those already having pelvic surgery.

milestones.label: Fewer cancer deaths beyond people already having pelvic surgery
milestones.explanation: A controlled trial would have to show fewer deaths from the targeted cancer among people recruited beyond those already having pelvic surgery. This would establish that prevention saves lives.

milestones.label: Pregnancy outcomes demonstrate preserved fertility through the tubes
milestones.explanation: Reproductive outcomes would have to show retained fertility through the tubes among participants attempting conception. Keeping tubes or ovaries alone would not establish this benefit.

milestones.label: Lasting prevention without unacceptable tissue injury
milestones.explanation: Treatment would have to reach the intended precursor and durably prevent progression without unacceptable tissue injury. This would connect its action to lasting protection and reproductive safety.

milestones.label: Independent teams reproduce benefit across clinical settings
milestones.explanation: Independent teams would have to reproduce benefit across clinical settings with clear eligibility and follow-up procedures. Reported limits would establish who benefits, access requirements and remaining cancer risk.

uncertain: Can dangerous precursors be reached and distinguished from changes that would never progress, early enough to prevent invasive cancer?
Which treatment could provide lasting protection while preserving the tubes’ reproductive function?
What follow-up, fertility measures and acceptable harms would make a trial’s result convincing?

page.title: Fertility-preserving interception of high-grade serous carcinoma
page.definition: An intervention stops a fallopian-tube precursor, a cell lesion preceding invasive high-grade serous tubo-ovarian carcinoma, while retaining conception through functioning tubes. Controlled studies demonstrate fewer deaths from this cancer and preserved reproductive outcomes.

goal.need: Tube removal provides observational evidence for prevention but cannot retain the removed tubes’ reproductive function. In UKCTOCS, screening increased stage I–II disease incidence by 39.2% without significantly reducing ovarian/tubal cancer deaths among 202,562 postmenopausal women after median follow-up of 16.3 years. The goal joins prevention before invasion with retained fertility.

statements.body: National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine
statements.quote: Improving the prevention and early detection of ovarian carcinomas will be a critical component of reducing morbidity and mortality from ovarian cancer.
Clinicians should include this prevention intervention in preoperative counseling of eligible women.
statements.context: The intervention is opportunistic salpingectomy: removal of fallopian tubes during unrelated surgery. This recommendation does not establish a tube-preserving intervention.

statements.body: Society of Gynecologic Oncology and American Society for Reproductive Medicine
statements.quote: Women at risk for hereditary gynecologic cancers have unique concerns regarding fertility and hormonal health.
statements.context: The joint review addresses cancer prevention, family building and the reproductive consequences of risk-reducing surgery.

completion.title: Precursor interception reduces HGSC deaths while preserving live birth through retained tubes.
completion.criterion: A prospective controlled study of treatment directed at a tubal precursor before invasion meets prespecified criteria for lower high-grade serous carcinoma mortality and preserved fertility. Fertility is evaluated using live births after conception through retained tubes among participants attempting pregnancy, against an appropriate comparator. Enrolment includes people recruited outside unrelated pelvic surgery. No external effect-size target, statistical cutoff, fertility margin or follow-up duration was found for this combined test; these require a registered protocol.
completion.set_by: Technology Atlas; provisional composite test without an identified external setter.
completion.basis: Searches of NASEM prevention recommendations, ESGO consensus statements, NCI prevention programmes, SGO/ASRM guidance and ClinicalTrials.gov found no published test combining precursor interception, tubal fertility and HGSC mortality reduction. The composite is an Atlas fallback. UKCTOCS supports mortality assessment because its stage shift did not significantly reduce deaths; the fertility requirement distinguishes this capability from tube removal.

milestones.title: A drug reduces invasive tubal adenocarcinoma in mogp-TAg mice at P ≤ 0.05.
milestones.criterion: The published assay compares drug and vehicle in groups of 10 genetically engineered mogp-TAg mice treated at 5 weeks and assessed at 8 and 12 weeks. Histology must show less invasive tubal adenocarcinoma at the study’s significance threshold, P ≤ 0.05. In the report published in 2022, depot medroxyprogesterone acetate reduced invasive cancers at 12 weeks from 8/10 controls to 2/10 treated mice (P = 0.005). The experiment did not establish mating success, live birth or a mortality benefit.
milestones.set_by: Nelson and colleagues, published animal-study protocol in Cancer Prevention Research. This test is specific to the mogp-TAg model.
milestones.threshold_quote: p-values of 0.05 or less were considered statistically significant.

milestones.title: A tubal-interception drug is administered to a human participant under an effective IND.
milestones.criterion: For a US investigational-drug route, a participant receives the intervention in a monitored Phase 1 study under an effective investigational new drug application (IND). An IND ordinarily takes effect 30 days after FDA receipt unless placed on clinical hold, or earlier on FDA notification. This establishes human exposure, without establishing preventive effectiveness or reproductive safety. The cited regulations are general drug-development criteria.
milestones.set_by: US Food and Drug Administration, 21 CFR 312.21(a)(1) and 312.40; general criteria for investigational drugs.
milestones.threshold_quote: Phase 1 includes the initial introduction of an investigational new drug into humans.

milestones.title: A drug shows preliminary human effectiveness against its intended tubal precursor.
milestones.criterion: For a drug-development route, controlled Phase 2 studies provide preliminary evidence of effectiveness for the intended tubal-precursor indication and characterize common short-term risks before Phase 3. FDA specifies no tubal-specific response cutoff. In the 2019 GOG-0214 report, 64 women received levonorgestrel or placebo for 4–6 weeks before tube-and-ovary removal. Neither tissue showed a significant apoptosis change; secondary nuclear-morphology changes did not establish precursor elimination or fertility preservation.
milestones.set_by: US Food and Drug Administration, 21 CFR 312.21(b)–(c); general clinical-development criterion applied to the drug route.
milestones.threshold_quote: preliminary evidence suggesting effectiveness of the drug has been obtained

milestones.title: A controlled study reduces invasive HGSC incidence while retaining tubal conception leading to live birth.
milestones.criterion: A prospective controlled study meets prespecified criteria for reduced invasive high-grade serous carcinoma (HGSC) incidence and retained live birth after tubal conception. The study published on February 2, 2026 instead compared 40,527 tube-removal patients with 45,296 comparators: crude serous-cancer hazard ratio 0.22 (95% CI, 0.05–0.95), with ≤5 versus 21 events. It combined low- and high-grade serous cancers, measured incidence and removed the tubes; it does not satisfy this composite.
milestones.set_by: Technology Atlas fallback. Searches of ESGO recommendations, SGO/ASRM guidance, NCI prevention programmes and trial registries found no published combined incidence-and-tubal-fertility criterion.

not_found: No published external criterion was located for the combined mortality-and-tubal-fertility completion test or the incidence-and-tubal-fertility milestone.
No controlled human result was located demonstrating precursor interception, retained tubal conception and reduced HGSC mortality together.
The GOG-0214 protocol PDF and full paper could not be opened; its peer-reviewed abstract was readable in the University of Arizona repository.
The 2026 ESGO consensus was readable at abstract level; its full recommendation text was not accessible.
